What a Structural Scope Should Cover Before You Build

A BOQ helps plan quantities and cost, but it is not a structural design. Use this checklist to prepare for a qualified engineer's site-specific scope.

Intextify Editorial Team5 min readEducational content
In this guidePrepare the inputsUseful scopeCompare with a BOQQuestions to ask

Start with the information the engineer needs

Bring plot dimensions, architectural drawings, proposed floors, intended room use, site photographs, and any soil or boundary information. This prevents an early estimate from being mistaken for a final design. If the plot has unusual soil, a slope, a basement, or an adjacent deep excavation, ask whether additional investigation is required.

What to expect in a useful scope

  • Foundation assumptions and the information used to select them.
  • Member drawings and a clear schedule for slabs, beams, columns, footings, and reinforcement.
  • Concrete and steel specifications, cover requirements, and details for openings and staircases.
  • Coordination notes for plumbing sleeves, electrical openings, water tanks, and later modifications.
  • A revision process: who approves changes and how drawings are reissued.

Use the BOQ as a comparison tool

Once drawings are issued, use a BOQ to compare like-for-like quotations. Keep the drawing revision, material grade, unit, quantity, waste allowance, transport, and labour scope beside each line item. A cheaper quote that excludes shuttering, testing, or cartage is not necessarily cheaper after work starts.

Questions worth asking before work begins

Ask which drawings are approved for construction, who will answer site queries, how substitutions are documented, and whether the contractor will provide bar-bending schedules and concrete test records. Put answers in writing.

Important: This is a planning checklist, not engineering advice. Engage a licensed, qualified professional for structural design and local approvals.
